title: Polynomial testing of induced four-cycle freeness
formal: Do there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that the canonical sampling test below, with sample size \[s(\varepsilon)=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil,\] rejects every finite simple graph that is \(\varepsilon\)-far from having no induced four-cycle with probability at least \(2/3\), for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)? The constants must be independent of the graph order and of \(\varepsilon\). The test always accepts graphs with no induced four-cycle, so this asks for polynomial-query one-sided testing in the dense graph model.
why: This is the unresolved concrete case, up to complementation, in the classification of polynomial testing for a single forbidden induced graph. It asks whether a globally expensive repair necessarily leaves violations visible in a polynomial-sized random sample. The answer would separate two very different quantitative regimes of dense-graph testing for one small and fully specified pattern.
status_note: Source-open as Conjecture 3.6 in the 23 August 2025 survey and in the paragraph after Theorem 1.1 of the checked Gishboliner–Shapira author manuscript. progress.text: Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, the graphs with no induced four-vertex path, and identify induced four-cycle freeness as the remaining single-pattern case up to complementation.

Goldreich poses the general polynomial-query classification question as Open Problem 8.26. This is the inherited source direction; the present concrete target was chosen later with explicit user authorization.

Gishboliner–Shapira's Theorem 1.1 proves that a graph far from induced-four-cycle freeness contains at least \(n^{4}/2^{(1/\varepsilon)^{c}}\) induced copies for an absolute constant \(c\), under their distance convention. The paragraph immediately following the theorem conjectures a polynomial improvement. The May 2018 author revision and the 2019 journal publication are distinguished.
The Polynomial Property Testing survey explicitly restates the polynomial induced-four-cycle conjecture as Conjecture 3.6, alongside the almost complete single-pattern classification in Theorem 3.5.

Carenini–Seth–Yoshida give a quantitative container characterization of size-oblivious one-sided testing. The checked Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.7 do not establish the polynomial bound for this specific induced pattern.

sentences: The question asks whether induced four-cycle freeness can be tested from a random sample whose size is polynomial in reciprocal proximity.
An induced four-cycle has its four cycle edges and neither diagonal, and repairing the graph permits both edge additions and deletions.
The canonical tester rejects when its sampled induced subgraph contains such a cycle and must reject every far graph with probability at least two thirds.
An exponential removal bound is known, while the polynomial improvement remains explicitly conjectured in the checked 2025 source.
This concrete target was selected with user authorization from the broader inherited classification question and would settle its remaining single-pattern case up to complementation.

definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\) is a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. An induced four-cycle consists of four distinct vertices \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\) whose edges among those vertices are exactly \(\{v_1,v_2\},\{v_2,v_3\},\{v_3,v_4\},\{v_4,v_1\}\); the two diagonals are absent. Let \(\mathcal P_n\) be the graphs on \([n]\) with no such induced subgraph. Define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\min_{([n],E')\in\mathcal P_n}|E\mathbin{\triangle}E'|.\] Here \(\triangle\) is symmetric difference, so both edge additions and deletions are allowed and each undirected edit is counted once. The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. The graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far when \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. This uses the edge-count-over-\(n^{2}\) convention of the selected survey; it is half the adjacency-matrix-entry distance in the original Goldreich question. The tester is given \(n\) and rational \(\varepsilon\), and has oracle access to the adjacency bit of any unordered vertex pair. For a positive integer \(s\), the canonical test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries every unordered pair in \(S\), and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced four-cycle. All \(\binom{\min\{n,s\}}{2}\) adjacency queries count; the property check on the finite sampled graph has no additional query cost, and no running-time bound is requested. Uniform subset sampling is the stated finite probability distribution, with sampling and local computation not charged as adjacency queries. If \(n\le s\), the entire graph is inspected. In particular, orders below four are always accepted and never far. No behavior is required for nonsatisfying graphs at distance at most \(\varepsilon\). Every host graph is allowed; no degree, density, chordality or other promise is imposed. The deterministic sampling-size formula and rejection rule specify a single uniform family of tests once \(C,a\) are fixed.
answer_criterion: Prove the formal proposition or its logical negation with a complete Lean-checked proof. A positive answer must exhibit fixed polynomial constants and establish rejection probability at least \(2/3\) for every far input and every permitted proximity parameter. A negative answer must show that for every choice of \(C,a\) there are a proximity parameter and a graph at the stated distance for which that sampling test rejects with probability less than \(2/3\). A merely exponential sample bound, a result for ordinary four-cycle freeness, or a tester with an additional host-graph promise does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: An induced four-cycle is a cycle without either diagonal. A complete graph on four vertices contains ordinary four-cycles, but no induced four-cycle. This distinction changes both the set of valid graphs and the repair task: adding a diagonal can destroy an induced cycle, while adding edges cannot eliminate an ordinary subgraph copy.

The tester does not try to find every violation or to reconstruct a repaired graph. It distinguishes graphs satisfying the property from graphs requiring more than \(\varepsilon n^{2}\) edits. A polynomial sample bound would mean that the number of queried adjacencies remains polynomial in reciprocal proximity even when the host graph is arbitrarily large.

The induced removal lemma relates edit distance to the number of forbidden induced copies. For a fixed pattern, polynomial bounds on that density and polynomial bounds for canonical one-sided sampling are equivalent up to changes in polynomial exponents. The known four-cycle removal bound is exponential in a power of reciprocal distance, which is far larger than the polynomial dependence conjectured here.

Alon and Shapira classified the polynomial and superpolynomial cases for single forbidden induced graphs apart from a few small patterns. Alon and Fox settled the four-vertex-path case, leaving the induced four-cycle and its complement as the remaining case. Complementing all adjacencies preserves edit distance and transfers the sampling question between those two patterns.

On 15 September 2026 the user authorized replacing the inherited classification programme by a concrete narrower statement. The selected target is Conjecture 3.6 of the 2025 survey. Goldreich's Open Problem 8.26 concerns all dense-graph properties, permits two-sided error, and asks for a characterization; it is strictly broader in scope and is not asserted equivalent to this testability conjecture. The separate active finite-family classification card also remains a different target.

The 2026 container characterization connects one-sided tester complexity to quantitative combinatorial parameters. It supplies an equivalence, rather than polynomial values of those parameters for every particular property. Consequently, the existence of that characterization does not itself settle the induced-four-cycle bound.
